newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany economy seen hit by tax reform failure.
newsitem.headline: Germany economy seen hit by tax reform failure.

text.p: Germany is headed for a tough time attracting investment and fighting unemployment after Bonn's tax reform proposal withered in a parliamentary deadlock, business leaders and analysts said on Thursday.
"The chance was wasted to make Germany more attractive in international competition for investment," Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said in a statement.

A parliamentary mediation committee, dominated by the opposition Social Democrats (SDP), rejected Finance Minister Theo Waigel's 30 billion mark ($16 billion) tax-cutting package in the early hours of Thursday.
Waigel said he wanted the mediation committee to reconvene in September to try again to hammer out a compromise, but the SPD said they would also reject his proposals then.
The proposed cuts would have taken effect mainly in 1999, after the two key years on which the fiscal performance of European Union states preparing for economic and monetary union would be judged.
The subject now looks set to turn into a major campaign issue in the runup to general elections in autumn 1998 and could drive a wedge into Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition.
"This is a disadvantage for Germany as a place of doing business," Rolf Peffekoven, a member of Bonn's council of economic advisers, told West German Radio.
Analysts said companies groaning under high rates of corporate taxation may now consider abandoning Germany for other European countries with lower tax rates.

"This big tax gap is an invitation for companies to look at transferring profits to other countries if possible, which means the investment cycle will be weaker in Germany and the labour market could continue to have problems," Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank in London, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).

Hans Peter Stihl, head of the German Federation of Chambers of Commerce (DIHT), said the SPD opposition was "a slap in the face to the economy". Cutting the trading tax, which had collected nine billion marks from businesses, "was only a drop in the bucket," Stihl said.
The only issue in the sweeping package of reforms the mediation committee managed to agree on was the ending of a five billion mark capital trading tax on companies.

Martin Kohlhaussen, President of the Association of German Banks and Commerzbank AG's chairman, lashed out at Bonn's politicians for having gambled away reforms that were pivotal for the country's economic health.

"The failure of the tax reform is a declaration of bankruptcy over Germany's ability to reform. It is irresponsible that the chance of a fundamental new start has been wasted because of party political manoeuvering," he said.
Chase's Redeker said the collapse of the reforms, which also included a cut in the solidarity surcharge levied to help rebuild eastern Germany, could endanger Kohl's coalition.
"With the solidarity tax on ice again differences between the coalition partners could increase in the autumn," he said.
Junior coalition partners the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) have staked their political future on a two percent cut in the solidarity tax to 5.5 percent next year.
But Ulrich Schroeder, senior economist at Deutsche Bank in Frankfurt, said Kohl would do all he could to avoid a split in the coalition, which could force early elections.

"After the election victories for the socialists in Britain and France nobody wants to have an early vote," Schroeder told RFTV. "But I think they will have to give something to the liberals -- at least a one percent cut in the solidarity tax."
